learning_goals: Explain what an LLM is and its limits
Define RAG and each word in the name
Describe the three steps retrieve augment generate
List benefits and one limitation of RAG

analogy.story: A student sits for an open‑book exam. The student first looks up the right page in the book, then writes the answer using that page.
analogy.mapping: Looking up the page is retrieval. Writing the answer from the page is generation.

worked_example.setting: A college student in Delhi uses a chatbot on the college website to ask about a government scholarship.
worked_example.question: What is the last date to apply for the PM Scholarship 2024?
documents: PM Scholarship 2024: Application opens 1 Jan 2024, closes 31 March 2024.
Eligibility: Indian citizens, family income below 8 lakh.
worked_example.retrieved: PM Scholarship 2024: Application opens 1 Jan 2024, closes 31 March 2024.
worked_example.answer_with_rag: The last date to apply is 31 March 2024, according to the official scheme document.

sections.heading: What You Will Learn
sections.goal: Show the main topics of the lesson
points: You will learn what an LLM is (F1)
You will learn LLM limits such as knowledge cutoff and no private data (F2, F3)
You will learn that LLMs can hallucinate (F4)
You will learn what RAG stands for (F5)
You will learn the three steps retrieve augment generate (F8)
You will learn benefits like fresh data and sources (F11)
You will learn one limitation about retrieval quality (F12)

sections.heading: Before We Start: Some Basic Ideas
sections.goal: Explain AI, LLM, and LLM limits in simple words
points: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on huge text (F1)
It predicts the next token (a word or part of a word) (F1)
Its knowledge stops at a fixed date called knowledge cutoff (F2)
It does not know private or organisation data (F3)
It can make up answers that sound confident, called hallucination (F4)

sections.heading: What Is RAG?
sections.goal: Define RAG and each word in the name
points: RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation (F5)
Retrieval means finding relevant pieces of information (F5)
Augmented means adding those pieces to the prompt (F5)
Generation means the LLM writes the answer using the added pieces (F5)
RAG does not change the model weights (F9)

sections.heading: Why Does RAG Matter?
sections.goal: List the main benefits of using RAG
points: Answers can use up‑to‑date information (F11)
Answers can use private or organisation data (F11)
Fewer made‑up answers, though not zero (F11)
Answers can show sources (F11)
Cheaper and faster than retraining the model (F11)
Knowledge is easy to update by changing documents (F11)

sections.heading: How Does RAG Work?
sections.goal: Explain preparation and the three question‑time steps
points: Preparation: collect documents, split into chunks (small pieces) (F7)
Turn each chunk into an embedding (a list of numbers that captures meaning) using an embedding model (F7)
Store embeddings in a vector database (a searchable index of vectors) (F7)
Question time step 1 retrieve: turn the user question into an embedding and find the most similar chunks (F8)
Step 2 augment: place the retrieved chunks into the prompt with the question (F8)
Step 3 generate: the LLM writes the answer from the prompt (F8)
The LLM weights stay the same, unlike fine‑tuning which changes weights (F9, F10)
Only a limited amount of text fits in the context window (F12)

sections.heading: Example: College Scholarship Query
sections.goal: Show a concrete Indian scenario with and without RAG
points: Setting: a Delhi student asks a college chatbot about a scholarship (worked_example)
Question: last date to apply for PM Scholarship 2024 (worked_example)
Documents in the knowledge base (worked_example)
Retrieved snippet gives the correct date (worked_example)
Plain LLM hallucinates a wrong date (worked_example)
RAG answer uses the retrieved snippet and cites the source (worked_example)

sections.heading: Key Words to Remember
sections.goal: List important terms with one‑line meanings
points: LLM – large language model, predicts next token (F1)
Token – a word or part of a word (F1)
Knowledge cutoff – date after which the model knows nothing (F2)
Hallucination – confident but wrong answer (F4)
RAG – retrieval-augmented generation (F5)
Retrieval – finding relevant chunks (F5)
Augment – adding chunks to the prompt (F5)
Generation – LLM writes answer (F5)
Chunk – small piece of a document (F7)
Embedding – list of numbers representing meaning (F7)
Vector database – index that stores embeddings for fast search (F7)
Fine‑tuning – extra training that changes model weights (F10)
Context window – max text the model can see at once (F12)

sections.heading: Quick Check
sections.goal: Test understanding with a few questions
points: What does RAG stand for?
Which step comes first: retrieve or generate?
Does RAG change the model weights?
Name one benefit of RAG.
What happens if the retrieved chunk is wrong?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.goal: Recap the whole lesson in a few lines
points: An LLM predicts tokens but has a knowledge cutoff and can hallucinate (F1‑F4)
RAG adds a retrieval step before generation so the model uses fresh or private data (F5, F8)
Preparation builds a vector database of chunk embeddings (F7)
At query time the system retrieves, augments, then generates (F8)
RAG does not retrain the model; it is cheaper and easier to update (F9, F11)
The answer quality depends on the quality of retrieved chunks (F12)

quiz.q: Which step comes first in RAG: retrieve or generate?
Does RAG change the model weights?
quiz.a: No, RAG does not change the model weights.
It lets the model use up‑to‑date or private information.

quiz.q: What happens if the retrieved chunk is wrong?
quiz.a: The answer can be wrong because the model relies on that chunk.
